**Pharmacology:** the scientific study of how drugs interact with living systems — from the molecular level to the whole patient.
**Drug (medication):** any chemical substance used to diagnose, treat, cure, or prevent disease, or to alter a physiologic process.
**Pharmacologic effect:** a measurable biological change a drug produces (e.g., lower blood pressure).
**Therapeutic effect:** the intended, beneficial pharmacologic effect for a given condition.
**Adverse drug reaction (ADR):** an unintended and harmful response occurring at normal therapeutic doses.
**Toxicity:** harmful effects that occur as the dose or exposure exceeds the therapeutic range.
**Chemical name:** describes the exact molecular structure (rarely used in clinical practice).
**Generic name:** the official, non-proprietary name assigned to the active drug — one generic name per drug, regardless of manufacturer.
**Brand (trade) name:** the manufacturer's marketed name; the same generic drug may have several brand names, and brand names change between countries.
**Prodrug:** an inactive precursor converted to the active drug in the body (usually by metabolism).
**Poisons** are drugs with almost exclusively harmful effects — but "the dose makes the poison" (Paracelsus): any substance can harm at the wrong dose.
Pharmacokinetics = what the body does to the drug — ADME.
Pharmacodynamics = what the drug does to the body — receptors & effect.
Pharmacogenomics = how genetic variation shapes individual drug response.
Clinical Pharmacology / Toxicology = applying PK/PD to real patients, and the study of poisoning.
This map covers the whole lecture: PK and PD are the two biggest buckets, and nearly everything else (toxicology, pharmacogenomics, therapeutics) sits on top of them.
**PA students should learn and prescribe by generic name — it is unambiguous, international, and avoids confusing a patient's multiple brand-name products for different drugs.**
Different brand-name products (Tylenol, many combination cold/flu products) can share the same active generic ingredient.
Prescribing and counseling by generic name avoids hiding duplicate therapy — the reason PAs default to generic names.
If a patient says they take "Tylenol" and separately "acetaminophen," check for accidental double-dosing — this previews the acetaminophen toxicity discussion.
Precise vocabulary (generic names, therapeutic vs. adverse effects) protects patients.
More than half of prescriptions in the USA are for generic drugs.
Acetaminophen (generic) is sold as Tylenol and under many store brands.

ADR = **A**t normal **D**oses, **R**eaction is harmful. Toxicity = **T**oo much (exceeds the therapeutic range).
**Efficacy:** how well a drug works under ideal, controlled trial conditions.
**Effectiveness:** how well a drug works in everyday clinical practice, with real-world adherence and comorbidities.
Drug interactions can also reduce real-world effectiveness below trial efficacy.
**Benefit vs. risk:** the central question regulators and prescribers must weigh for every approval and every prescription.
**Adverse-event reporting:** ongoing, voluntary and mandatory reporting systems (e.g., FDA MedWatch) that catch safety signals after approval.
Where new drugs come from — Natural products: plants, fungi, microbes, marine organisms.
Synthetic & biotech: designed small molecules; recombinant proteins.
Biologics: monoclonal antibodies, gene- and cell-based therapies.
Drug repurposing: an existing approved drug found to treat a new condition.
From discovery to patient: Discovery → Preclinical testing → Clinical trials → FDA review → Approval → Postmarket surveillance.
Most candidate drugs fail somewhere along this pipeline — approval is the exception, not the rule.
Phase I: safety, tolerability, dose-finding — a small group of healthy volunteers.
Phase II: preliminary efficacy and side-effect profile — a few hundred patients with the target condition.
Phase III: confirm efficacy and monitor adverse effects at scale — hundreds to thousands of patients, often multi-site.
Phase IV: postmarketing surveillance after approval — the general prescribed population.
Every approved drug has passed through a structured development and regulatory pipeline (Phases I–IV).
Phase II has the **highest failure rate** — only about 25% of new drugs move on to Phase III.
Phase III usually enrolls **thousands** of patients (Figure 1–6: 1000–6000), often double-blind and crossover, in settings like the drug's eventual use.
Less than one-third of drugs studied in humans survive clinical trials and reach the market.
To see one case of a toxicity occurring 1 in 10,000, several hundred thousand patients may need exposure — so rare effects usually surface only in Phase IV, which has **no fixed duration**.
Marketing requires a **New Drug Application (NDA)** after Phase III; human testing starts only after an **IND** (Investigational New Drug) application.
Postmarketing surveillance (Phase IV) is where rare adverse effects are often first detected — trial populations are too small and too short in duration to catch 1-in-10,000 events.

Case: a new medication improves symptoms in 70% of patients with a chronic, non-life-threatening condition, but postmarketing data show serious hepatotoxicity in about 1%. **Would you prescribe it — and does your answer depend on what else is available?**

**Clinical pearl:** risk-benefit analysis is always comparative — a 1% serious-toxicity rate reads very differently if it is the only effective option versus if three safer alternatives already exist.
Ask "compared to what?" rather than judging the number in isolation.
A patent lasts 20 years; after it expires, generics are approved through an **abbreviated new drug application (ANDA)** that requires bioequivalence data.
Placebo responses can occur in as many as 30–40% of subjects — the reason controlled, blinded trials are needed.
Adverse events that are both **serious and unexpected** must be reported to the FDA within 15 days; clinicians can report through MedWatch.
FDA MedWatch — an adverse-event reporting system.

**Drug target:** the specific molecule a drug binds to produce its effect.
**Receptor:** a protein target whose activation (or blockade) triggers a cellular response.
**Signal transduction:** the chain of molecular events that converts receptor binding into a cellular effect.
**Pharmacologic response:** the measurable downstream result — contraction, secretion, gene transcription, and so on.
Full agonist — maximal receptor activation.
Partial agonist — submaximal activation, even at full receptor occupancy.
Inverse agonist — reduces baseline (constitutive) receptor activity.
Competitive antagonist — reversibly competes with agonist at the same site; overcome by more agonist.
Noncompetitive antagonist — binds elsewhere or irreversibly reduces the maximal effect.
Irreversible antagonist — permanently inactivates the receptor until new receptor is synthesized.
The pathway: drug → target → signal transduction → response. Every pharmacodynamics topic for the rest of the course maps onto this chain.
Receptor concept: Drug + Receptor → Drug-Receptor Complex → Cellular Response.
This single chain underlies agonism, antagonism, potency, and efficacy — all describe different features of this interaction.
Five major drug target classes: receptors, ion channels, enzymes, transporters, nucleic acids.
Receptors: G-protein-coupled, ligand-gated ion channel, enzyme-linked, nuclear.
Ion channels: directly gate the flow of ions across a membrane.
Enzymes: drugs can inhibit or, less commonly, activate an enzyme's activity.
Transporters & nucleic acids: carrier proteins; or DNA/RNA for some antimicrobials & gene therapies.
Most drugs target receptors or enzymes — ion channels and transporters matter especially for cardiac and CNS drugs.
An inverse agonist actively reduces constitutive (baseline) receptor activity below normal; a true antagonist merely blocks the agonist without lowering baseline activity itself.
**Spare receptors:** a maximal response can occur without occupying every receptor (e.g., about 90% of cardiac β receptors can be blocked and maximal inotropic response still preserved).
**Irreversible antagonist** effects last until new receptors are made — duration depends on receptor turnover, not drug elimination (phenoxybenzamine for pheochromocytoma).
A partial agonist's lower maximal effect is **not** due to lower affinity — it can occupy all receptors and still produce less response.
**Allosteric modulators** bind a different site from the agonist (e.g., benzodiazepines enhance GABA's effect).
Agonist-induced **desensitization** (tachyphylaxis) and downregulation reduce response with continued exposure.
Albuterol is a selective β2-adrenergic receptor agonist.
Binding activates the β2 receptor → increases intracellular cAMP.
Rising cAMP relaxes bronchial smooth muscle → bronchodilation.
**This is the same receptor-to-response logic you will reuse for every agonist drug this term.**
Albuterol bridges introductory pharmacodynamics into the pulmonary pharmacology seen later in the curriculum.
Competitive antagonism is surmountable in real life: exercise or stress raises catecholamines enough to overcome a fixed propranolol dose.
Propranolol markedly slows the heart rate in pheochromocytoma (high catecholamines) but not the resting rate of a trained marathon runner.
Albuterol — selective β2-adrenergic agonist (example of agonism).

t: Classic exam trap: a competitive antagonist shifts the dose-response curve **right** (same Emax, more drug needed); a noncompetitive/irreversible antagonist **lowers the Emax** instead.

t: Why can more agonist overcome a competitive antagonist? Both compete **reversibly for the same site** — flood the site with agonist and it wins, so the curve shifts right but the same Emax is still reached.
Why does albuterol open the airways? β2 activation → ↑ intracellular cAMP → bronchial smooth muscle relaxes → bronchodilation.
**C**ompetitive = **C**an be outcompeted (shift right). **N**oncompetitive = **N**o full ceiling (lower Emax).
**Potency:** how much drug is required to produce a given effect — a more potent drug needs a lower dose.
**Efficacy (Emax):** the maximum effect a drug can produce, no matter how high the dose goes.
**EC₅₀:** the drug concentration producing 50% of the maximal effect — the standard measure of potency.
**Therapeutic Index (TI) = TD₅₀ ÷ ED₅₀ (toxic dose in 50% ÷ effective dose in 50%).**
**Quantal dose-response:** ED₅₀ (effective in 50%), TD₅₀ (toxic in 50%), LD₅₀ (lethal in 50% of animals).
**Therapeutic window:** the range between the minimum therapeutic dose and the minimum toxic dose — more practical than TI for dosing a patient.
The sigmoidal dose-response curve: x-axis = log(dose), y-axis = effect. EC₅₀ is on the x-axis; Emax is the plateau — the ceiling effect.
EC₅₀ is read off the curve at the halfway point between baseline and Emax.
Lower EC₅₀ = more potent. Higher Emax = more efficacious.
Potency and efficacy are independent properties — a drug can differ in one without differing in the other.
A curve farther left reaches the same effect at a lower dose (greater potency); curves reaching the same plateau height have identical Emax (efficacy).
A wide TI means a large margin between an effective dose and a toxic dose — generally safer to dose.
A narrow TI means effective and toxic doses are close together — requires careful dosing and often blood-level monitoring.
The distance between the ED₅₀ and TD₅₀ markers is the therapeutic index itself.
Dose-response curves describe potency and efficacy.
Potency clinically matters for dosing — not for choosing the "better" drug.
Efficacy clinically matters much more than potency — a highly potent drug with low efficacy may be clinically useless.
With a narrow TI, a small dosing error can move a patient from effective to toxic — which is why these drugs require blood-level monitoring.
Students should be able to name all four narrow-TI drugs without hesitation and know that each requires therapeutic drug monitoring.
No drug causes only a single specific effect — drugs are **selective**, not specific.
Asthma + hypertension on propranolol: nonselective β blockade can cause bronchoconstriction; a β₁-selective blocker (metoprolol) is an alternative.
**Classic narrow-TI drugs: warfarin, lithium, digoxin, phenytoin.**

t: Why do narrow-TI drugs need blood levels? The effective dose and the toxic dose sit so close together that a small dosing error can push the patient from effective to toxic.
Why does efficacy beat potency clinically? Potency only changes the dose you give; efficacy sets the ceiling of what the drug can achieve at any dose.

TI = **T**oxic over **E**ffective → TD₅₀ ÷ ED₅₀ (toxic on top).
A — Absorption: movement of drug from the site of administration into the bloodstream.
D — Distribution: movement of drug from blood into tissues.
M — Metabolism: chemical transformation of drug, mainly in the liver.
E — Excretion: removal of drug/metabolites from the body, mainly via the kidney.
**Bioavailability (F) = the fraction of an administered dose that reaches systemic circulation unchanged.**
First-pass effect: the liver metabolizes (can inactivate a large fraction of) an orally absorbed drug before it reaches systemic circulation.
**Volume of distribution (Vd):** a calculated value relating total drug in the body to plasma concentration — a high Vd suggests extensive tissue distribution.
ADME is the organizing skeleton for the rest of the lecture — each remaining pharmacokinetics section is one ADME letter in depth.
ADME determines how much drug reaches its target and for how long.
Metabolism (M arrow → liver) and Excretion (E arrow → kidney) are the back half of ADME — how the body gets rid of the drug; Absorption and Distribution govern how the drug arrives and spreads.
First-pass route: oral drug → GI tract → portal circulation → liver → systemic circulation.
By definition, an IV dose has 100% bioavailability — the entire dose enters the bloodstream directly (no absorption step).
Oral bioavailability is reduced by incomplete absorption and by first-pass hepatic metabolism.
**Plasma protein binding:** only unbound ("free") drug is pharmacologically active and able to cross membranes.
**Lipid solubility:** lipophilic drugs cross membranes more readily and distribute into fatty tissue.
**Tissue perfusion:** highly perfused organs (brain, heart, kidney) receive drug faster than poorly perfused tissue (fat, bone).
Vd is a theoretical volume, not a real anatomic space.
Blood-brain barrier — **Why can some drugs readily enter the CNS while others cannot?** Tight junctions between endothelial cells restrict paracellular movement.
Small, lipophilic, non-ionized drugs cross the BBB more easily than large, polar, or highly protein-bound drugs.
Efflux transporters (like P-glycoprotein) can actively pump some drugs back out of the CNS.
**P-glycoprotein (MDR1)** pumps drugs out of cells in brain, testes, and gut; inhibiting it raises digoxin blood levels.
Ion trapping: weak acids are excreted faster in **alkaline** urine; weak bases faster in **acidic** urine.
Routes that bypass first-pass metabolism: essentially everything except oral — IV, sublingual, inhaled, transdermal, topical, SC, IM.
Sublingual absorption enters systemic venous circulation directly, bypassing the portal vein and the liver's first-pass metabolism; oral dosing passes through the liver first.
Because the liver can inactivate a large fraction of drug first, some drugs are given sublingually or transdermally instead of orally.
A highly polar antibiotic would generally not cross the BBB well — unless the meninges are inflamed, as in meningitis.
Aspirin overdose: sodium bicarbonate alkalinizes blood and urine, reducing aspirin entry into tissues and speeding its renal excretion.
Large first-pass effect: nitroglycerin, propranolol, morphine — all require higher oral doses (or a non-oral route) to achieve the same systemic exposure as IV.

Drug metabolism = how the body chemically transforms drugs.
Phase I — Functionalization: oxidation, reduction, hydrolysis.
Phase II — Conjugation: glucuronidation, sulfation, acetylation, methylation, glutathione conjugation.
**Enzyme inhibition:** a drug slows a CYP enzyme, raising the blood level of any drug that CYP normally clears.
**Enzyme induction:** a drug increases CYP enzyme production, lowering the blood level (and effect) of drugs that CYP clears.
Why metabolize? To inactivate an active drug, making it easier to excrete.
To activate a prodrug into its active form.
To produce an active metabolite that contributes to (or extends) the drug effect.
**Occasionally to produce a toxic metabolite — the basis of some drug-induced organ injury.**
Phase I is primarily carried out by cytochrome P450 (CYP450) enzymes and often creates or unmasks a reactive functional group.
Phase II attaches a polar group to the molecule, producing a more water-soluble product for renal/biliary excretion.
Phase I often comes before Phase II, but not always — some drugs go straight to conjugation.
Inhibition slows clearance (substrate level rises); induction speeds clearance (substrate level falls).
CYP3A4 alone metabolizes over 50% of the prescription drugs metabolized by the liver.

**Example: Drug A inhibits CYP3A4 → Drug B (a CYP3A4 substrate) accumulates → toxicity risk rises.**
Inhibition pushes a substrate's level ABOVE 100% of baseline (toxicity risk); induction pushes it BELOW 100% (therapeutic-failure risk).
Inhibiting the CYP that clears a substrate is especially dangerous when the substrate has a narrow therapeutic index.
Enzyme induction speeds substrate clearance, lowering its level and effect — the opposite of inhibition.
Liver disease (e.g., cirrhosis, hepatitis) slows metabolism of some drugs enough that ordinary doses can cause coma.
Severe ADRs contribute to about 100,000 US deaths a year and about 7% of hospital admissions.

Metabolism inactivates drugs, activates prodrugs, or makes active or **toxic metabolites** (e.g., NAPQI); **Phase I** (CYP450 oxidation, reduction, hydrolysis) functionalizes and **Phase II** conjugates for excretion.
A **CYP inhibitor raises** a substrate's level (toxicity) and an **inducer lowers** it (therapeutic failure) — always check CYP450 interactions before adding a drug.
The **kidney** is the main elimination route — filtration of free drug, active secretion, reabsorption of lipophilic un-ionized drug — and less renal function means less clearance and more exposure.
**Half-life** (time for concentration to fall 50%) depends on clearance and Vd: ~**4–5 half-lives** to steady state and ~**97%** eliminated after ~5.
**Loading doses** (based on Vd) reach the target immediately; **maintenance doses** (based on clearance) keep levels in range; in CKD adjust dose and/or interval by eGFR/CrCl.

**Pharmacogenomic** variants (CYP2D6, CYP2C19, TPMT, HLA-B*5801) change drug response, but genotype is one input in a checklist of indication, contraindications, organ function, interactions, patient factors, and dose/route/monitoring.
